newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries narrowly mixed as Greenspan awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries narrowly mixed as Greenspan awaited.

text.p: The prices of Treasury securities closed narrowly mixed Tuesday on the eve of testimony by the U.S. central bank chief.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan begins testifying before the Senate at 1000 EST/1500 GMT Wednesday and a mood of nervousness prevailed on Wall Street where players feared he might say something that hinted at imminent tightening of monetary policy.
The 30-year bond closed unchanged at 99-19/32 to yield 6.66 percent.

The market had traded in positive ranges throughout much of the session, but fell lower after a disappointing two-year note auction. Treasury sold $17.5 billion of two-year notes at midafternoon that met little demand. Traders said volume was light, though there was a late day spurt of activity.

"I was surprised the market held up as well as it did. I certainly don't expect Greenspan to say anything constructive for the market," said Ian Shepherdson, chief U.S. economist for HSBC Markets Inc. "I find it hard to envisage that after Humphrey-Hawkins we don't have to worry about interest rates any longer."

Shepherdson pointed to continuing high levels of consumer confidence, noting that January levels were revised upward in this session's report. The Conference Board said consumer confidence slipped only slightly in February to 118.4, from a revised reading of 118.7 in January. The present situation index rose more than two points to 143.4, a 27-year high.

"The story for a long time is that we haven't had a surge in (consumer) spending based on the surge in the stock market, which has gained another 7.0 percent since he made comments in December," Shepherdson said.
These factors pointed to potentially strong growth ahead.
"The market is hoping he argues the economy slows in the second half of the year due to the strength of the dollar. But he needs to cite some reason he sees the economy slowing," Shepherdson said.
Shepherdson didn't see a lot of upside for fixed-income securities with expectations that housing would rebound, car sales improve and labor markets getting tighter.

"There should be no major surprises so the bond market should take (Greenspan's testimony) in stride following some backup in yields in anticipation of more hawkishness," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.

Jones said Greenspan could be expected to allude to acceleration in wage pressures and the abundance of liquidity on a global basis. But he saw only moderate hawkishness from the Fed chairman with no sense of urgency about tightening.

"Bottomline, the watchful waiting period continues and he continues to say we have to watch wage levels and product prices. My sense is he may go along lines similar to the December 17 FOMC policy record," Jones said.
Jones said minutes from December's FOMC meeting revealed a protracted discussion of stock market valuations and could prompt more talk of the situation by Greenspan.
Treasury will sell $12.5 billion of five-year notes Wednesday. In when-issued trade on Tuesday, five-year notes ended with a 6.187 percent yield.
Three-month bill rates rose one basis point to 5.02 percent. Six-month bill rates were two basis points lower at 4.99 percent and year-bill rates were one basis point higher 5.20 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 1/32 at 100-even, yielding 5.87 percent. Five-year notes closed at 100-08/32, down 2/32, yielding 6.19 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 98-31/32, down 1/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
